title: Modular Scripting: Sourcing Files 📦
description: Organise reusable functions into separate files and include them with `source` or `.`.

slides.title: Don't Repeat Across Scripts 📚
slides.content:
## Your Own Library

If you have a killer logging function, you don't want to copy‑paste it into every script. Put it in a separate file and **source** it.

Sourcing runs the commands in the current shell, so any functions (or variables) defined there become available in your script.

slides.title: Create a Library
slides.content:
File: `logger.sh`
```bash
log_info() {
  echo "[INFO] $(date): $1"
}
```
Main script:
```bash
source logger.sh
log_info "Script started"
```
slides.codeSnippet:
# Create logger.sh first:
# echo 'log_info() { echo "[INFO] $(date): $1"; }' > logger.sh
source logger.sh
log_info "Hello from main"

quizData.question: Which command(s) can be used to include another Bash file?
quizData.explanation: `source filename` or `. filename` (dot space filename) includes the file in the current shell.

slides.title: The Dot Command ➿
slides.content:
## `.` is an Alias for `source`

The `.` (dot) command does exactly the same thing:
```bash
. ./lib.sh
```
It's shorter, but `source` is more readable to newcomers. Both are correct.

slides.title: Organising a Library
slides.content:
A typical structure:
```
project/
  main.sh
  lib/
    ui.sh
    backup.sh
```
`main.sh`:
```bash
source lib/ui.sh
source lib/backup.sh
```
slides.codeSnippet:
mkdir -p lib
echo 'print_header() { echo "==== $1 ===="; }' > lib/ui.sh
source lib/ui.sh
print_header "Welcome"

quizData.question: Sourcing a file runs it in a new subshell, isolating variables.
quizData.explanation: No, sourcing executes the file in the **current** shell, so any changes to variables or functions affect the current script.

slides.title: Finding the Right Path 📍
slides.content:
## Relative vs Absolute

- `source ./lib.sh` – relative to current working directory.
- `source /path/to/lib.sh` – absolute.
- Use `$(dirname "$0")` to source files relative to the script's own location.

Example:
```bash
DIR="$(cd "$(dirname "$0")" && pwd)"
source "$DIR/lib/utils.sh"
```

slides.title: Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content: Check if the library file exists before sourcing: `[ -f "lib.sh" ] && source lib.sh || { echo "Missing lib"; exit 1; }`.
